candidates.text: He stood in the wet grass and looked at it for a long time, long enough for the wind to find the gap between his collar and his neck, long enough for the lamp above him to sweep once across the headland and find him standing there, small and deliberate, at the base of a door that had no business being there. The sea had been eating that cliff for a hundred years; it had taken the stair, the winch-house, the graves of three keepers whose names were still cut into the memorial wall up top. Salt had done this to everything it touched, and yet the door was dry. That was the first wrong thing. The second was the brass handle, worn to a soft shine on the side a hand would grip, though no hand had gripped it since the water came in and took the rest of the cliff path. He tried the latch. It turned. Cold air came out of the dark below, carrying a smell he knew from his childhood but could not immediately name — lamp oil, and stone, and something faintly like bread. He had not brought a lantern. Above him, the great lens began its slow rotation, laying its pale beam across the sea, and for a moment the door's brass caught the light and threw it back at him, and he saw, just for an instant, that the hinges were oiled. Recently. As if someone, very patiently, had been keeping it.

He found it on the way down, where the path cut into the rock for the oil store: a door of seasoned oak, iron-banded and salt-bleached grey, set flush into the granite as though the cliff had been quarried around it. No weeds grew at its base. No drip of rust stained the hinges, and the sill, he noticed with the small cold certainty that comes only to men who have lived alone a long time, was swept clean. He had walked that path four thousand times and knew every stone of it; the door was not new, but it had not been there the day before, and there was no explaining that, so he did not try. His hand went to the latch. It was warm — not sun-warm, for the sun had not touched that wall since noon, but warm the way a thing is warm when it has been closed over a fire for a long while. It turned without a creak. Cold air breathed out around the frame, carrying lamp oil, wet wool, and something sweeter beneath it, like honey. And from somewhere in the dark beyond, patient and unhurried, a clock was ticking.

He had walked this path two hundred times a year for eleven years, and in that time he had learned every contour of the cliff — the seam of white quartz that ran through the stone like a vein, the shallow hollow where rain gathered, the ledge where the gulls nested in spring. So he knew the door was wrong before he touched it. It sat flush in the rock face, old oak banded with iron, and it belonged to no century he knew: the hinges were newer than the lighthouse itself, the wood darker than the wet stone around it, as though it had been waiting there for the salt to eat it down. There was no handle, only a keyhole cut in the shape of a circle with seven points inside it. And from the seam where rock met wood, a thin thread of air came out — cold, moving, smelling of lamp oil and something else beneath it, something sweet, like flowers kept in a cellar. Above him the great lens began its nightly turn, dragging its beam out across the water, and for a moment the light swept the door and turned the iron bands to silver. He did not reach for it. He had spent his life keeping watch over what came out of the dark, and he knew with the certainty of a man who reads weather in the color of the sea that this door was not meant to be opened from the outside. Or that it was — but not tonight, and not by him alone.

task.brief: A lighthouse keeper finds a door in the cliff below the lamp room that was not there yesterday. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the door implies a consequence the keeper must act on
the paragraph keeps the sea and the lamp in view
something is at stake for the keeper personally
task.reference_text: The keeper set the oil can down and counted the door twice, the way he counted ships. It was blue, salt-blistered, and hinged on the seaward side, which meant whoever built it had worked from the water.
